<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
I've read it closely and checked the figures. This is a well-constructed follow-up:
- It answers the three open questions it set itself.
- It adds a stricter hours measure.
- It registers the mediation test before the outcome data existed.
- It is candid about the Halden subset being "survivors twice over."

Its corrections to the earlier pieces are mostly right:
- The four long-follow-up studies in the meta-analysis being uncontrolled and using scheduled hours confirms the problem with its "no decay" claim.
- An 8.5% gain under the standards Varga and Holm recommended refutes "entirely an artifact."

There are, however, a few issues that bear directly on the headline numbers.

## Arithmetic checks

- **Varden, timesheet hours:** 0.966 / 0.88 = +9.8% ✓
- **Varden, log hours:** 0.966 / 0.89 = +8.5% ✓
- **Halden continuers:** 34.9 / 40.3 = −13.4%, and 0.968 / 0.866 = +11.8% ✓

## Major issues

**1. The Summary mixes measures when describing the decline.**
- The Summary says the per-hour gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months."
- But 12.5% is on timesheets and 8.5% is on system logs.
- The like-for-like comparison, which the body correctly identifies, is 12.5% → 9.8%: a fall of about a fifth, not a third.
- Part of the apparent decline is just the change of measure. The error makes the result look more conservative, but the Summary should still compare like with like.
- The decline itself is also imprecise. The 9-month CI (6.9 to 18.4) and the 24-month CI (4.6 to 15.2) overlap heavily. "Consistent with some fading" is the right phrasing, and it should be carried into the Summary and §5.

**2. The control group was contaminated, and that may explain part of the "fading."**
- In month 15, two control offices carried out a meeting audit and their output per hour rose about 4%.
- That raises the control comparison and pulls down the difference-in-differences estimate for months 15–24.
- So some of the decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may reflect improvement in control offices, not erosion in treated ones.
- It is also worth asking whether the audit was prompted by the trial's own nine-month report, which publicised the meetings finding. If so, this is spillover from the evaluation itself.
- Two analyses would resolve this:
  - re-estimate with those two offices excluded or censored from month 15;
  - report the treated and control per-hour trajectories separately, so readers can see which arm moved.

**3. The 47% meetings figure may partly be accounting rather than mechanism.**
- If the hours denominator includes meeting time, cutting meetings raises output per hour automatically, even if nothing changes in how case work is done.
- A rough calculation from the reported figures suggests this effect could be large. Assume timesheet hours of about 37.9 at baseline in both arms, with treated hours 12% lower at 24 months:

| | Baseline non-meeting hours | 24-month non-meeting hours | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Treated | 37.9 − 7.4 = 30.5 | 33.4 − 3.9 = 29.5 | −3.3% |
| Control | 37.9 − 7.2 = 30.7 | 37.9 − 7.0 = 30.9 | +0.7% |

- That is roughly a 4% relative fall in non-meeting time, set against a 3.4% fall in output per FTE. Output per non-meeting hour would then be close to unchanged relative to control, at around +0.5%.
- If that holds, removing meeting time accounts for nearly all of the per-hour gain, not 47%. That would leave little room for the 18% attributed to fatigue or the 35% unexplained.
- The calculation depends on assumptions the paper doesn't confirm, so it may not hold. Two things would let readers check it:
  - **Define what the system logs capture.** The paper describes them as "time staff are working on cases." If that is literally true, logs exclude meetings, and an 11% fall in logged hours is hard to square with non-meeting time falling only about 4%. If logs record session time, including while staff sit in meetings, they are not a stricter measure of work, just a different measure of presence.
  - **Report output per non-meeting hour directly.** This separates "meetings were removed from the denominator" from "removing meetings made the remaining hours more productive" (less fragmentation, more focus). Both are real gains to the employer, but they are different mechanisms with different implications. In particular, the first is available to any organisation that cuts meetings, whatever its hours.

**4. The registered mediation test confirms the hypothesis on the same units that generated it.**
- Registering the test at month 11, before the 24-month data existed, is good practice.
- But the hypothesis came from the same seven treated offices, so this is a prospective test on the same units, not an independent replication.
- "A larger sample of office-months" doesn't increase the number of independent units, which is still 14 clusters.
- Two further points:
  - The meetings CI (28 to 66%) needs the same small-cluster correction I raised for the nine-month report. The method should be stated.
  - The no-unmeasured-confounding assumption is acknowledged, but matters here. Offices whose managers cut meetings most may differ in other management practices that also raise output.

**5. The registered primary outcome gets less prominence than the per-hour results.**
- Output per FTE was the registered primary outcome. Its point estimate drifted from −2.1% to −3.4%, and the upper CI bound fell from +2.6 to +1.2.
- That is still not statistically distinguishable from zero. But it is moving toward a loss, and it is what the county pays for.
- The Summary leads with per-hour results. It should lead with the primary outcome.

## Smaller points

- **Earlier gaps are still open:**
  - Backlog size and time to decision are still not reported. The nine-month report flagged these as risks, and they are the natural check on whether −3.4% per FTE is accumulating as delay.
  - Overtime cost and cost per case are still absent, although the counter arm gets a cost estimate.
  - Appeal overturn rates are again levels without pre-period values or CIs.
- **Counter cost estimate.** The +9% cost per contact is plausible. With 12% more staff, hours of about 0.93 of the original and the +6.7% per-hour gain roughly restore capacity. A 12% rise in labour costs would then translate to about 9% per contact if labour is around three-quarters of total cost. The derivation should be stated.
- **Halden subset:**
  - The subset was selected three times: organisations that had records, then those that agreed to provide data (14 of 23), then those that continued (11 of 14). The authors label it an upper bound, which is correct.
  - One of the three reverting organisations was a marketing agency, which presumably counted as discretionary work. Client deadlines can make nominally discretionary work coverage-bound, which supports the meta-analysis's caveat about binary work-type coding.
- **Authorship.** The follow-up is co-authored by an author of the original Halden working paper, whose attrition reporting Varga and Holm showed to be inaccurate. The Halden section here is appropriately cautious. A brief statement acknowledging the earlier misreporting would still help readers.
- **The meeting-audit observation.** It is handled well: clearly caveated, and it raises the right policy question of reorganisation alone versus reorganisation plus fewer hours. It is also an uncontrolled before–after comparison with no seasonal adjustment, so the 4.1% figure carries the same weaknesses as the pilots.

## Overall

The main conclusions are supported:
- In backlog work, a randomised per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% persists to two years, somewhat smaller than at nine months.
- Output per worker is close to maintained but slightly lower.
- Coverage-bound work could not sustain the change.

The open questions have shifted:
- **Novelty:** the gain persists, so "is it novelty?" is largely answered.
- **Mechanism:** "Is the gain more productive hours, or fewer unproductive ones?" is not yet answered. The answer could be "mostly the latter."
- **Hours cut versus meeting reduction:** "Does the hours cut add anything beyond cutting meetings?" remains open. The paper names this question honestly. Answering it would need a trial arm that reorganises without reducing hours.

Fixing the Summary's measure comparison and handling the control contamination should come first. Reporting output per non-meeting hour comes next: it may change the story more than anything else here.
